commons:201237925.summary: Set behind an elaborate gilded Rococo grille, this small wooden statue shows the Virgin seated with the Christ Child held before her, both with long, solemn faces. Venerated for centuries in the abbey church of Remiremont, the 11th-century image has been framed and adorned by later generations as a treasured relic of the abbey's past.
facts: It has been classified as a historic monument (objet classé) since 20 June 1907.
The French heritage database dates the carved wooden statue to the 11th century and notes that it has been dressed in rich fabrics.
According to the Commons record, it is about 68 cm high.
commons:201237925.notes: The photograph shows the statue at a distance behind its gilded grille, so details are hard to make out.

cur:objects-berlin-entry-into-jerusalem-.summary: Beneath an arcade Christ rides sideways on a donkey toward the gate of Jerusalem, followed by his disciples, while the people come out to meet him, children spread garments in his path and a boy climbs a tree to cut branches. The scene is carved in deep relief with many small figures, yet Christ's calm, upright figure remains the clear focus. In the Byzantine cycle of feasts this image announced Palm Sunday and the beginning of the Passion.
facts: The panel was the centre of a triptych; its wings, now lost, would have folded over it to protect the image (type).
The Entry into Jerusalem was one of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Byzantine Church, frequently represented on ivories and icons (type).

cur:objects-douce-ivory-book-cover.summary: In the centre Christ stands triumphant, carrying a cross over his shoulder and a book, trampling the lion, dragon, asp and basilisk. Twelve small surrounding panels narrate episodes from the Gospels, beginning with the Annunciation and Nativity and including miracles of Christ. The composition proclaims the victorious Lord whose earthly life, told around the edges, accomplished the defeat of evil.
facts: Wikipedia's article on Christ treading on the beasts calls it the 'Oxford book cover' and notes its four beasts, the full set named in the Vulgate verse.
The book it covers is MS Douce 176, measuring about 21 × 12 cm.
